extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art history; general educated readers interested in Greek sculpture
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and aesthetic principles for judging classical Greek sculpture (especially Myron, Polycleitus, and related works), focusing on movement, rest, proportion, naturalness, purpose, and expressive restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness / 'The natural is ever best!'
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalness is the supreme aesthetic value: 'The natural is ever best!' — a work that embodies the unconscious perfection of youth and the unspoiled body is triumphant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalness may mean the work suggests no new view but embodies an ideal (like a perfect flower). Learned or elaborate manner is acceptable only if subordinated to this natural effect; naturalness delights the viewer as an unconsciously felicitous state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of movement (mastery of motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful sculpture captures voluntary animal motion and the 'soul' of movement (e.g., Myron's Discobolus: 'the very soul is undoubtedly there' in the motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for the union of opposing motions, the moment between two actions ('rest in motion'), and the sense that the form is about to move — the artist's ability to translate fleeting motion into enduring form is a core merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of rest (mastery of repose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equally important is the depiction of rest after exertion (Polycleitus's Diadumenus as exemplar): the passive beauty and serenity of a victor at rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the sculptor conveys restful form, the harmony of static laws, and the contemplative aftermath of action; restraint and the pleasure of perfected rest are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between physical (anima) and rational (animus) expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists differ in rendering the 'animal' (physical) soul and the 'reasonable' (mental) soul; Myron 'did not express the sensations of the mind—animi sensus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether expression of mind would harm the youthful bodily ideal; sometimes disavowing overt mental expression preserves the purity and fairness of the bodily soul, while a latent capacity for thought may still be present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of youthful beauty (avoidance of pathos that ages youth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal athlete should not display the pathos or expressive signs that would make him no longer youthful; pathos often contradicts the proper expression of youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether emotive or intellectual expression intrudes upon the youthful form and thus undermines the work's purpose of celebrating unspoiled youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of ornament/learned technique to artistic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Even 'learned involution' or elaborate technical manner is 'laudable' if it is subordinated to the work's purpose as an object to be seen rather than thought about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that technical complexity serves the visual and emotional aim of the piece and does not draw attention away from its primary appeal as an object of sight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon / Proportion / 'Measure of Man'
rubrics_metrics.description: The establishment and fidelity to a canon of proportion (Polycleitus's 'measure' or common standard of the perfect man) is a key evaluative standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the harmony of proportions, static laws, and whether the figure exemplifies the proposed ideal; recognize that the canon aims at mortal youthful perfection rather than any supersensual ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence of parts (head, body, physiognomy belonging together)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of a sculpture must be congruous—heads and bodies should belong together physiognomically and in spirit (the British Museum Discobolus head 'does not really belong to the discobolus').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for mismatches in vigor, expression, or proportion between parts that disrupt the unity and intended effect of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survivals of archaism and conventionalism (appropriate primitive elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survivals of primitive manner (e.g., hair treatment, attenuated limbs) may be congenial if congruous with the work's overall style; such archaism can have its own attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether archaic features harmonize with the piece (adding charm or authenticity) or feel incongruous with the artistic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre, purpose, and function (portrait, votive, decorative, commemorative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding whether a work is portrait, type, votive offering, or decorative genre piece is essential to its evaluation and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the intended purpose (commemorative, decorative, votive, genre) — this contextualizes choices of realism, idealization, and detail, and influences judgment of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious or civic significance influencing form
rubrics_metrics.description: Athletic sculptures often carry religious or civic meanings (athletics as a form of worship), which colors their pose, modesty, and symbolic attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ritual or symbolic aspects (e.g., crowns as sacred prizes) when assessing pose, restraint, and the moral/aesthetic tone of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional restraint, modesty, and absence of vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Valued works exhibit modesty and restrained delight in themselves rather than vanity—purity of expression and absence of affectation are praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the piece conveys a 'glowing, yet restrained joy' and lacks ostentation; restraint often indicates cultural ideals of temperance and worship of the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of form and implied motion (metaphysical equilibrium)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful sculpture embodies the metaphysical mystery of combined motion and rest, creating an equilibrium where matter 'rests' yet the form 'scarcely more' rests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for the artistic achievement of making static material convey dynamic trajectory and potential energy—the sense that the object is both at rest and in motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical finish and attention to detail (graving, after-thoughts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical refinement—chiseling, fine engraving, and after-thoughts (Polycleitus was 'renowned as a graver')—is a mark of self-exacting craftsmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the quality of finish and subtle detailing as indicators of the sculptor's discipline; such finish should enhance, not overpower, the overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle emotional tone (melancholy, wistfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A faint, pagan melancholy or wistful awareness may survive in athletic types, contributing a deeper, blended impression beyond mere physical delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note subtle affective shades (wistfulness, capacity for thought) that add complexity to otherwise youthful, restrained figures and affect the viewer's lasting impression.
